content.intro: This lesson develops topic 206 of the supplied curriculum: **The NumPy C API**. The main starting point is **Reasons for using the C API**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Compiled extensions and stride-level operations can improve specialized workloads but increase portability and memory-safety complexity. Learn the high-level array contract first and keep extension paths narrowly tested.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **The NumPy C API** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Reasons for using the C API** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.title: Subtopics from the supplied curriculum
items: Reasons for using the C API

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype=np.float64)
print(a.shape, a.dtype, a.flags.c_contiguous)

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: The C API is a specialist boundary for extensions, not required for everyday NumPy. Memory ownership, dtype layout, strides, reference management, and NumPy version compatibility matter.

common_mistakes.problem: Using low-level memory tools without validating strides and bounds
common_mistakes.why: Strided views and extension interfaces depend on layout and ownership contracts.
common_mistakes.fix: Start with safer high-level functions and add targeted tests before low-level paths.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming compiled binaries work across major NumPy versions
common_mistakes.why: The C API has binary-compatibility concerns across major versions.
common_mistakes.fix: Build/test wheels against supported NumPy versions and review migration notes.
